source.title: Topographic Training Concentrates Causal Circuits Without Improving Neuron Monosemanticity
source.authors: Gautam Ranka; S. Pandere; Aiden Dsouza

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates superposition-related representation and circuit measures in topographically trained vision transformers, a new setting and with different methods from the toy-model source. It does not test the specific conditions in any listed version.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own SAE, neuron-selectivity, activation-patching, and spatial-coherence results. These concern representation complexity and circuit organization, but do not test the listed versions' specific claims about toy-model geometry, capacity as the cause of polysemanticity, LLM representations, SAE features as canonical units, or one-dimensional features.
record.test_reason: The study adopts the superposition hypothesis as framing and uses SAE L0 and dead-feature fraction as a proxy for superposition. It then reports how its own training intervention (TopoLoss) shifts these measures in vision transformers. It does not test any listed version. There is no toy-model sweep (V1) and no test of capacity as the cause of polysemanticity (V2) or of alternative causes (V3). The models are ViTs, not LLMs (V4), and the study runs no stability or canonicity checks on SAE features (V5) and no test of feature dimensionality (V6). The reader's 'tests/T3' contradicts its own note that no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also frame the L0 drop as 'reduced feature superposition' and conclude that neuron-level monosemanticity metrics may be insensitive to circuit-level interpretability gains. They position TopoLoss as a cheap training-time complement to post-hoc tools.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a TopoLoss training intervention on vision transformers, followed by SAE measurements and activation patching; it does not use the toy-model feature construction or geometry analysis of the original.
record.method_sensitivity: Effects depend on α: α = 0.1 does not reliably change SAE L0, dead-feature fraction, or spatial coherence, while α = 1.0 does in ViT-S/16. TinyViT's H3 ratio peaks at α = 0.1 and does not improve at calibrated α = 0.38 or α = 1.0. Main analyses use layer 6.

fits_no_version.finding: In ViT-S/16 at α = 1.0, SAE L0 drops 11% and the dead-feature fraction rises 19-fold. Neuron-level and SAE-feature-level class selectivity stay flat, and the L0 drop is partly confounded with accuracy (R² = 0.72).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In vision transformers, a topographic training loss can lower SAE-measured feature density without changing per-neuron or per-SAE-feature class selectivity.

fits_no_version.finding: In ViT-S/16, the cluster/random patching ratio rises monotonically with α (1.68 to 2.27 to 2.79). Spatial concentration is significant only at α = 1.0.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Topographic training concentrates the causal influence of class-activated unit sets into spatially local clusters in ViT-S.

fits_no_version.finding: In a single-seed TinyViT run, L0 decreases slightly and monotonically. The patching ratio peaks at α = 0.1 (1.42×) and does not improve at calibrated α = 0.38.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: TopoLoss causal-cluster effects do not transfer consistently to a small 4-layer ViT.

record.peer_reviewed: Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, 2026
record.problems: The paper reports a partial accuracy confound for SAE L0: α = 1.0 reduces accuracy by 1.6 percentage points, and accuracy explains substantial L0 variance in an OLS analysis. An accuracy-matched ablation is left for future work. TinyViT results use one seed and cannot isolate depth, width, accuracy, or training-budget effects. Some reported selectivity comparisons are described as non-significant, and the α = 0.1 main L0/dead-feature numerical outcomes are not fully given in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible result rows were omitted. The paper also reports validation accuracy, PCA dimensionality, and weight-norm calibration; these are supporting confound or calibration analyses rather than measurements of the claim's representation or geometry outcomes.

untested.parts: No toy model and no sweep of sparsity, feature count or dimension. No analysis of feature geometry.
No test of whether capacity limits cause polysemanticity or whether important features get dedicated dimensions.
No test of non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
Only vision transformers are studied, not LLMs. SAEs are used as a diagnostic without validating that recovered features are the model's features.
No test of completeness, stability across seeds or dictionary sizes, or canonicity of SAE features.
No test of one-dimensional versus multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: The study measures its own intervention's effect on SAE metrics and uses superposition only as framing, so no verdicts are given. Rows not recorded include Table 5's SAE L0 values from the 25k-image re-run (1304/1316/1189), the layer-wise L0 curves, and TinyViT dead% and Mu (Table 9). None of these bear on a listed version.

versions.untested_parts: No toy-model sweep of feature count, sparsity, importance, dimensionality, or regular feature geometry.
Does not test whether limited capacity causes polysemanticity, or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions while others share.
Does not test alternative causes of polysemanticity or whether polysemanticity alone indicates superposition.
The models are vision transformers, not LLMs; the study does not establish that LLM activations are distributed across neurons or that SAE features recover their features.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of a model's representation.
Does not test whether represented features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional.
